Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 1–4:

(p-263) Surat Yasin is Meccan. From him (ﷺ) [it is related]: "Ya-Sin is called al-Mu'imma (the one that encompasses), for it encompasses its reciter in the good of both abodes; and al-Dafi'a (the one that repels) and al-Qadiya (the one that fulfils). It repels from him every evil and fulfils for him every need." Its verses number eighty-three.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ya-Sin﴾ is like ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ in meaning and in grammatical analysis (i'rab). It has been said that its meaning is "O man" (ya insan) in the dialect of Tayy, on the basis that its origin is "Ya Unaysin," and it was shortened to a part of it because of the frequent use of calling by it, as it has been said that ﴿min Allah﴾ [is shortened] in "Ayman" (in the oath formula). It is read with kasra, like "jir," and with fatha, as an indeclinable form like "ayna," or as an inflected form with "itlu Yasin" (recite Yasin), or with a hidden oath particle, and the fatha is due to the prohibition of diptotic inflection (man' al-sarf). It is also read with damma, indeclinable like "haythu," or inflected as "hadhihi Yasin." Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ruh and Abu Bakr made the ya' pronounced with imala (inclination). Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr, Warsh and Ya'qub assimilated the nun into the waw in ﴿wal-Qur'ani al-Hakim﴾, and that waw is either the waw of oath or the waw of conjunction if ﴿Ya-Sin﴾ is taken as the thing sworn by.

﴿Innaka lamina al-mursalin﴾ — [meaning] you are indeed among those who were sent.

﴿'Ala sirat mustaqim﴾ — and it is the Tawhid (oneness of God) and uprightness in affairs. It is permissible that ﴿'ala sirat﴾ be a second predicate or a circumstantial state (hal) of the implicit pronoun in the prepositional phrase. Its benefit is to describe the Law explicitly as upright, even though ﴿among the messengers﴾ indicates it by implication (iltizam).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 5–6:

﴿A revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the verbal noun (maṣdar) is in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ūl). Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Ḥafs read it in the accusative (naṣb), by supposing an implied verb "I mean" (aʿnī) or its verb, so that it stays in its original state. It is also read in the genitive (jarr) as an apposition (badal) to "the Qur'an."

﴿So that you may warn a people﴾ is connected either to "revelation" (tanzīl) or to the meaning of "you are among the messengers." ﴿Whose fathers were never warned﴾: a people whose fathers were not warned, meaning their nearer forefathers, because of the long period of interruption (fatrah) between messengers. In this case it is a descriptive clause (ṣifah mubayyinah) clarifying the intensity of their need for the sending of a messenger. Alternatively, "that which" (alladhī) refers to what they were warned with, or to "something with which their distant forefathers were warned," in which case it is a second object of "so that you may warn" (li-tundhira). Or it is the warning of their forefathers taken as a verbal noun. ﴿Therefore they are heedless﴾ is connected, on the first reading, to the negation, meaning: they were not warned, so they remained heedless. Or it is connected to the statement ﴿Indeed you are among the messengers﴾ on the other readings, meaning: We sent you to them so that you might warn them, for they are heedless.

It is said that the two verses were revealed about the Banu Makhzum: Abu Jahl swore that he would crush the head of the Prophet (ﷺ). Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 13–14:

﴿And set forth for them﴾ the likeness of the people of a town, as an example drawn from their own words; these things are on one pattern, that is, one example. The verb (ḍaraba) takes two objects, because it includes the meaning of "making" (ja'l), and they are: ﴿a parable, the companions of the town﴾, by omitting a noun (ḥadhf muḍāf), meaning: make for them the likeness (mathal) of the companions of the town a parable. It is also permissible to limit it to one object and to make the implied element a substitute (badal) for the stated one or an explanation (bayān) of it. The town (al-qarya) is Antioch. ﴿When the messengers came to it﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the companions of the town." The "messengers" (al-mursalūn) were the messengers of Jesus, peace be upon him, sent to its people. Its attribution to Himself in His saying ﴿when We sent to them two﴾ is because it is the act of His messenger and vicegerent. They were Yahya and Yunus, and it has been said that they were others than these two. ﴿But they denied them, so We strengthened﴾, that is, We reinforced. Abu Bakr recited it with light emphasis (mukhaffaf), from ʿazzahu, meaning he overcame him, and the object was omitted because what precedes it indicates it, and because the intended matter is the mention of that by which it was strengthened. ﴿with a third﴾, and he was Shamʿun. ﴿So they said, "Indeed we are messengers to you."﴾ That was because they were worshippers of idols, so Jesus, peace be upon him, sent two to them. When they drew near the city, they saw Habib the carpenter tending sheep, so they asked him and they informed him. He said: "Do you two have a sign?"

They said: "We heal the sick and cure the blind and the leper." He had a sick son, so they wiped over him and he was healed. Habib believed, and the news spread, and a great multitude was healed at their hands. Their report reached the king, and he said to them: "Do we have a god other than our gods?" They said: "Yes, He who brought you into being and your gods." He said: "I will look into your affair," and he imprisoned them. Then Jesus sent Shamʿun, who entered disguised and mixed with the king's companions until they became familiar with him and brought him to the king, and he became attached to him. One day he said to him: "I have heard that you imprisoned two men; have you heard what they say?" He said: "No." So he summoned them, and Shamʿun said: "Who sent you?" They said: "God, who created everything and has no partner." He said: "Describe Him and be brief." They said: "He does what He wills and decides what He desires." He said: "And what is your sign?" They said: "What the king wishes." So he called a boy whose eyes were blinded, and they called upon God until his sight split open for him, and they took two pustules (bundusatayn) and placed them in his eyeballs, and they became two eyes with which he looked. Shamʿun said: "Do you see? If you asked your gods to do the like of this, so that you and they would have honor?" He said: "I have no secret for you; our gods do not hear, do not see, do not harm, and do not benefit." Then he said: "If your God is able to bring a dead person to life, we will believe in Him." They brought a boy who had died seven days earlier, and they called upon God, and he stood up and said: "I was made to enter seven valleys of Fire, and I warn you of what you are in, so believe." He also said: "The gates of heaven were opened, and I saw a handsome youth interceding for these three." The king said: "Who are they?" He said: "Shamʿun and these two." When Shamʿun saw that his words had affected him, he advised him, and he believed along with a group. Whoever did not believe, Gabriel, peace be upon him, cried out at them, and they perished.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 18–19:

﴿They said: "Indeed we take omen from you."﴾ We consider you an ill omen (tashā'amnā bikum), and that is because of their astonishment at what they claimed, their finding it repugnant, and their aversion to it. ﴿"Indeed, if you do not desist"﴾ from this saying of yours, ﴿"we will surely stone you, and a painful punishment will surely touch you from us."﴾

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 22–24:

﴿And why should I not worship He who originated me?﴾ On the reading other than that of Hamzah, for he pauses on the yā’ (the letter ya) when reading continuously (wasl). It is a gentle manner of guidance, presenting it in the form of counsel to himself and sincere advice, since he wished for them what he wished for himself. The intent is to rebuke them for abandoning the worship of their Creator in favour of worshipping others. For this reason he said: ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾, as an intensification of the warning. Then he returned to the first line of argument and said:

﴿Shall I take besides Him gods, if the Most Merciful wills harm for me, their intercession will avail me nothing, nor will they save me?﴾ Their intercession will not benefit me at all. ﴿Nor will they save me﴾ by giving help and support.

﴿Indeed, I would then be in manifest error.﴾ For preferring what neither benefits nor averts harm in any way over the Creator, who is capable of benefit and harm, and associating others with Him, is a clear error that is not hidden from any sensible person. Nafi', Ya'qub and Abu 'Amr read the yā’ with a fatha.

﴿Innī āmantu bi-rabbikum﴾ (Indeed I have believed in your Lord), who created you. Nāfi', Ibn Kathīr and Abū 'Amr read it with a fatḥah on the yā' (i.e., ﴿bi-rabbiya﴾ is not the reading; rather the reading is with the yā' opened as "rabbī"). ﴿Fa-sma'ūn﴾ (So listen to me): listen to my faith. It is also said that the address is to the messengers, for when he advised his people, they began to stone him, so he hastened towards them before they could kill him.

﴿It was said: Enter Paradise﴾: it was said to him this when they had killed him, as glad tidings to him that he was among the people of Paradise; or as honour and permission to enter it like the rest of the martyrs; or, when they resolved to kill him, God raised him to Paradise, according to what al-Ḥasan said. He did not say "it was said to him" because the purpose is to state what was said, not who it was said to, since that is known. The statement is a resumption (istinaf), answering a question about his state upon meeting his Lord after his steadfastness in supporting his religion. Likewise: ﴿He said: Would that my people knew﴾.

﴿For what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honoured﴾: this is an answer to a question about what he said at that moment. He wished that his people knew his state so that they would be moved to acquire the like of it, by repenting of disbelief and entering faith and obedience, following the practice of the friends of God in restraining anger and showing mercy to enemies. Or so that they would know that they had been in grave error regarding his matter and that he had been upon the truth. It was also read as «al-mukarramīn» (the honoured). "Mā" may be a relative/noun-of-information (khabariyyah) or a verbal-source (maṣdariyyah) particle, and the bā' is connected to (ya'lamūn). Or it may be an interrogative (istifhamiyyah), used in its original form, and the bā' is connected to "ghafara": i.e., "for what (ghafara) to me," meaning by it the emigration from their religion and the patient endurance of their harm.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 29–30:

﴿In kānat﴾ meaning: it was not (anything other than) the seizing (al-akhdhah) or the punishment. ﴿Illā ṣayḥatan wāḥidah﴾ (only a single cry): Jibril (peace be upon him) cried it out, and it was also read as ﴿ṣayḥatun wāḥidatun﴾ with the nominative (raf‘), taking kāna as the complete (tāmmah) verb (i.e., "there occurred a single cry"). ﴿Fa-idhā hum khāmidūn﴾ (then they were extinguished): dead. They were likened to fire, as a symbol that the living is like a blazing flame and the dead is like its ash, as Labid said:

"And a man is nothing but like a meteor and its light... it turns to ash after it was blazing."

﴿Yā ḥasratan ʿalā al-ʿibād﴾ (Alas for the servants!): O (regret), this is one of the states in which you should be present, namely what is indicated by:

﴿Mā yaʾtīhim min rasūlin illā kānū bihi yastahzi'ūn﴾ (No messenger came to them but they used to mock him). The mockers of sincere advisers, upon whose counsel depends the good of both abodes, are deserving that they should regret and that regret should be felt for them. The angels and the believers of both the jinn and mankind have lamented their condition. It is also permissible that this is a regret from God concerning them, by way of metaphor (istiʿārah), to magnify what they inflicted upon themselves. This is supported by the reading ﴿Yā ḥasratā﴾ with a fatha on it, due to its length, by the prepositional phrase attached to it. It was also said that the verb is implied and the vocative particle is omitted. And it was read ﴿Yā ḥasrata al-ʿibād﴾ with the idafah (genitive construction) to the agent or the object, and ﴿Yā ḥasratan﴾ with a hāʾ (pausal form) "ʿalā al-ʿibād," treating the connected reading as if it were a pause.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 31–32:

﴿Have they not seen﴾ — i.e., have they not known — and it is suspended (mu'allaq) from his saying: ﴿how many generations We destroyed before them﴾, because (kam) does not have what precedes it act upon what follows it, even though it is informative (khabariyyah), since its origin is interrogative (istifham). ﴿That they, to Us, will not return﴾ is a substitute (badal) for (kam) in meaning, i.e., have they not seen the multitude of those We destroyed before them, that they are not returning to them? It is also read with a kasrah (i.e., innahum), as a resumption (isti'naf).

﴿And indeed, all of them, when brought together, will be present before Us﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, for judgment. (In) is a lightened form of the heavy (in), the lam is the one that distinguishes (al-lam al-fariqah), and (ma) is extra for emphasis. Ibn ‘Amir, ‘Asim and Hamzah read (lamma) with shaddah in the sense of (illa) ("except"), so that (in) is negative and (jami‘) is in the form fa‘il in the sense of maf‘ul ("gathered"), and (ladayna) is an adverbial of place (zarf) either for it or for (muhdarun).

And a sign for them is the dead earth. Nafi' read it with shaddah (intensive doubling), as ﴿الْأَرْضُ الْمَيْتَةُ﴾ is written. The phrase (أحْيَيْناها, ahyaynāhā, "We gave it life") is a predicate of (الأرْضُ, al-ardu, "the earth"), and the whole clause is the predicate of (آيَةٌ, āyah, "sign"). Alternatively, the clause may be a qualifier (ṣifah) of (āyah), since it does not refer to a specific sign. Or the clause may be the predicate (khabar), with (āyah) as the subject (mubtada'), and (āyah) then serves as the predicate of the clause. Or the clause may be a resumptive sentence (istinaf) explaining why it is a sign.

﴿وَأَخْرَجْنَا مِنْهَا حَبًّا﴾: "and We brought forth from it grain," meaning a kind of grain.

﴿فَمِنْهُ يَأْكُلُونَ﴾: "from it they eat." He placed the prepositional phrase (مِنْهُ, minhu, "from it") first, to indicate that grain is the main thing that is eaten and by which people live.

﴿وَجَعَلْنَا فِيهَا جَنَّاتٍ مِنْ نَخِيلٍ وَأَعْنَابٍ﴾: "and We placed in it gardens of palm trees and grapevines," meaning from the varieties of palm and grape. For this reason he joined the two in the plural, unlike grain, because a noun denoting a genus (jins) implies difference, whereas a noun denoting varieties (anwā') does not. He mentioned palm trees rather than dates (tumūr) so that it would match grain and grapes, since these trees are distinguished by greater benefit and evidence of craftsmanship.

﴿وَفَجَّرْنَا فِيهَا﴾: "and We caused springs to gush forth in it." It was also read with the lighter form (takhfīf). The verb (fajara, "to split open/gush forth") and its intensive form (tafjīr) are, both lexically and semantically, like (fataḥa, "to open") and (taftīḥ, "to open widely").

﴿مِنَ الْعُيُونِ﴾: "from the springs," meaning some springs. The qualified noun was omitted and the qualifying phrase was placed in its position. Alternatively, (al-'uyūn, "the springs") and (min, "from") are superfluous (zā'idah) according to al-Akhfash.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 36, verses 35–36:**

﴿So that they may eat of its fruit﴾: of the fruit of what was mentioned, which is the gardens. It was also said that the pronoun refers to God, Exalted is He, by way of *al-iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person), and the attribution to Him is because the fruit is by His creation. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *thamarihi* with two *dammas* (ثَمَرِهِ read as *thumurihi*), and this is a dialect form of the word. Alternatively, it is the plural of *thimar* (ثِمار), and it was read with one *damma* and a sukun (*thumri*).

﴿And what their hands made﴾: this is coordinated with "the fruit." The intended meaning is what is made from it, such as juice, *dibs* (date syrup), and similar things. It was also said that *ma* (ما) is negative, meaning that the fruit is by God's creation and not by their action. The first interpretation is supported by the reading of the Kufans other than Hafs, which omits the *ha'* (هاء) pronoun. Its omission from the relative clause is better than other options.

﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾: He commanded gratitude insofar as the question is a rebuke for abandoning it.

﴿Glory be to Him who created the pairs, all of them﴾: the kinds and the types. ﴿Of what the earth grows﴾: of plants and trees. ﴿And of themselves﴾: the male and the female. ﴿And of what they do not know﴾: and pairs of things God Most High has not informed them of, and for which He has not provided them a way to knowledge.

**Verse 37–38**

﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip off from it the day﴾: We remove it and uncover it from its place. The expression is a metaphor (isti'ara) borrowed from the stripping of skin (salkh al-jild). The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the verse is as discussed previously. ﴿Then they are in darkness﴾: they have entered into the darkness.

﴿And the sun runs on to a fixed resting place for it﴾: to a specific limit at which its cycle comes to an end. It is likened to the resting place of a traveller when he has completed his journey. Or it refers to the midpoint of the sky (kabd al-sama'), since its movement there slows so much that one supposes it has a pause there. The poet said:

*"The sun, bewildered, circles in the air."*

Or it refers to its settling upon a particular course. Or it refers to a determined end for each day among the risings and settings, for in its cycle the sun has three hundred and sixty risings and settings. It rises each day from one rising-point and sets at one setting-point, and then does not return to those two until the following year. Or it refers to the cessation of its motion at the ruin of the world.

It has been recited as «لا مُسْتَقَرَّ لَها» (*lā mustaqarra lahā*), meaning there is no rest for it, since it is constantly in motion. It has also been recited as «لا مُسْتَقَرَّ» (*lā mustaqarr*), with «لا» understood to mean "not" in the sense of *laysa*.

﴿That﴾: the running on this determined course, which contains wisdoms whose enumeration exhausts the discerning minds. ﴿is the decree of the Mighty﴾: the Victorious, who by His power prevails over every thing that can be decreed. ﴿the All-Knowing﴾: whose knowledge encompasses every object of knowledge.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 39–40:

﴿And the moon: We determined its course.﴾ We determined its motion. ﴿Stations﴾, or: We made it travel through stations, which are twenty-eight: al-Sharatan, al-Butayn, al-Thurayya, al-Dabaran, al-Hak'a, al-Han'a, al-Dhira', al-Nathra, al-Tarf, al-Jabha, al-Zubra, al-Sarfa, al-'Awwa', al-Simak, al-Ghafr, al-Zibana, al-Iklil, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Na'a'im, al-Balda, Sa'd al-Dhabih, Sa'd Bula', Sa'd al-Su'ud, Sa'd al-Akhbiya, Far' al-Dalw al-Muqaddam, Far' al-Dalw al-Mu'akhkhar, and al-Rishaa, which is the belly of the fish. Each night it descends into one of them, not passing beyond it and not falling short of it. When it is in its last station, where it is just before conjunction, it becomes thin and curved. The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿wal-qamara﴾ (and the moon) with the ra' in the accusative case (naṣb).

﴿Until it returns like the 'urjun﴾, meaning like the curved stalk of a palm cluster. The word 'urjun is of the pattern fu'lun, from al-in'iraj, which means bending. It is also read «al-'arjun», and both are dialectal variants, like al-buzyun and al-bazyun. ﴿Ancient﴾ means old. It is said it refers to what has passed over it a year or more.

﴿The sun: it is not fitting for it﴾, meaning it is not proper or easy for it, ﴿to overtake the moon﴾ in the swiftness of its course. For that would disrupt the growth of plants and the living of animals. Or it means overtaking its traces and benefits, or its place by descending to its position, or its authority, so that its light is obliterated. Placing the negative particle before the sun indicates that the sun is subjected, so nothing is possible for it except what is intended for it.

﴿Nor does the night outpace the day﴾, meaning it does not get ahead of it so as to leave it behind, but it follows it in succession. It is said the intended meaning is their signs, which are the two luminaries, and outpacing means the moon's advance into the sun's authority. This makes it the reverse of the first case. The word "outpacing" is used in place of "overtaking" because it suits the swiftness of the moon's course.

﴿And each﴾, meaning all of them. The tanwin (nunation) is a replacement for the omitted genitive noun. The pronoun refers to the suns and moons, since the difference of states requires a plurality in essence. Or it refers to the heavenly bodies, since mention of the two implies them. ﴿In an orbit they float﴾, meaning they travel in it with ease.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 48–50:

﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ They mean the promise of the resurrection (al-ba'th).

﴿They are not waiting for﴾ — ma yanzurun, meaning ma yantazirun (they are not awaiting). ﴿except a single blast﴾ — it is the first blast (al-nafkha al-ula) of the Trumpet. ﴿It will seize them while they are disputing﴾ — they will be disputing about their trade and their dealings, and the matter will not come to mind, like His saying: ﴿Or the Hour will come upon them suddenly while they do not perceive﴾. The original form is yakhtasimun. The ta' was made sukun and assimilated (idgham, merging a letter into the next), then the kha' was given a kasra because of the meeting of two sakin letters (two consecutive unvowelled letters). Abu Bakr read it with a kasra on the ya' for harmony with the following vowel (al-ittiba', vowel harmony). Ibn Kathir, Warsh and Hisham read it with a fatha on the kha', by transferring the vowel of the ta' to it (ilqa' harakat al-ta'). Abu 'Amr and Qalun read it likewise but with ikhtilas (a rapid, truncated articulation of the vowel). From Nafi' there are three readings: fatha, sukun, and tashdid (doubling). It seems he permitted joining two sakin letters when the second is assimilated. Hamza read yakhissimun, from khasamahu, meaning when he argued with him (jadalahu).

﴿So they will not be able to make any bequest﴾ regarding any of their affairs. ﴿Nor will they return to their families﴾ so that they may see their condition; rather, they will die where the blast overtakes them.

﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾, i.e., a second time, and its explanation has already been given in Surah al-Mu'minun. ﴿Then, behold, from the graves (al-ajdath)﴾, from the tombs, plural of jadath; it is also recited with the letter fa' (al-ajdaf). ﴿They will hasten forth to their Lord﴾, i.e., they will rush; it is also recited with a dammah on the letter ya'.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 51–52:

﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾, i.e., a second time, and its explanation has already been given in Surah al-Mu'minun. ﴿Then, behold, from the graves (al-ajdath)﴾, from the tombs, plural of jadath; it is also recited with the letter fa' (al-ajdaf). ﴿They will hasten forth to their Lord﴾, i.e., they will rush; it is also recited with a dammah on the letter ya'.

﴿They will say: "Woe to us!"﴾ It is also recited "Woe to us" with a fatha on the ta' (yā waylatanā). ﴿"Who has raised us up from our resting place?"﴾ It is also recited "Who has roused us?" (man ahabbana), from habba, meaning one who wakes up from his sleep when he becomes alert; and man habbana has the same meaning as ahabbana. In this there is tarshih (a suggestive hint), remote allusion, and an indication that, because their minds are confused, they imagine that they had been asleep. The readings "man ba'athana" and "man habbana" are with min as a preposition and the verbal noun (masdar). Hafs alone paused on it with a slight pause (sakta latifa), and stopping on it in all other readings is acceptable (hasan).

﴿"This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth."﴾ It is a mubtada' and khabar, and ma is either a verbal (masdariyya) particle, or a relative pronoun (mawsula) with a deleted returning pronoun; or "this" is an attribute of "our resting place," and "what the Most Merciful promised" is the khabar of a deleted subject; or it is a mubtada' whose khabar is deleted, i.e., "this is what the Most Merciful promised and the messengers spoke the truth"; or "what the Most Merciful promised and the messengers spoke the truth is true," and it is from their own speech. It has been said that it is an answer from the angels or from the believers to their question, deviating from its usual form in order to remind them of their disbelief, to rebuke them for it, and to alert them that what concerns them is the question about the resurrection rather than the one who raises them. As if they were saying: "The Most Merciful, who promised you the resurrection and sent the messengers to you, has raised you, and they confirmed you; the matter is not as you suppose, for a sleeper is not raised, so the question about who raised you would not concern you. Rather, it is the Greatest Resurrection, full of terrors."

﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joy, reclining﴾ (fakihun), enjoying themselves with delight in the bounty. The indefiniteness and vagueness of (شُغُلٍ, shughul) magnify the joy and pleasure they are in, and indicate that it is higher than what minds can grasp and what speech can express the reality of. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr read (شُغْلٍ) with a sukun. Ya'qub, in one narration, read «فَكِهُونَ» (fakihun) for emphasis. Both are predicates of (إنّ, inna). It is also permissible for (في شُغُلٍ, fi shughul) to be a complement (صِلة, silah) of (فاكِهُونَ, fakihun). It was also read «فُكُهُونَ» (fukuhun) with a damma, which is a dialect like (نُطُسٍ, nutus) and (نَطِسٍ, natis). And «وَفاكِهِينَ» and «وَفَكِهِينَ» are read as circumstantial clauses (حال, hal) of the hidden pronoun (مُسْتَكِنّ, mustakinn) in the adverbial phrase. (شَغَلٍ, shaghal) with two fathas, a fatha and a sukun, are all dialects.

﴿They and their spouses are in shades﴾, plural of (ظِلّ, zill) like (شِعاب, shi'ab), or (ظُلَّة, zullah) like (قِباب, qiba'b). The reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i, «ظُلَلٍ» (zulal), supports this.

﴿On couches﴾: on the adorned thrones. (مُتَّكِئُونَ, muttaki'un) and (هم, hum) is a subject (مُبْتَدَأ, mubtada'), whose predicate is (في ظِلالٍ, fi zilal), and (عَلى الأرائِكِ, 'ala al-ara'ik) is a resumed sentence, or a second predicate, or (مُتَّكِئُونَ, muttaki'un), with the two prepositional phrases as its complements. Or it is an emphasis of the pronoun in (شُغُلٍ, shughul) or in (فاكِهُونَ, fakihun). (عَلى الأرائِكِ مُتَّكِئُونَ, 'ala al-ara'ik muttaki'un) is another predicate, because (أزْواجُهم, azwajuhum) is conjoined to (هم, hum) for sharing in the three rulings. And (في ظِلالٍ, fi zilal) is a circumstantial clause (حال, hal) of both the conjoined and the element it is conjoined to.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 57–58:

﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they call for.﴾ "Whatever they call for" (mā yaddaʿūn): that which they ask for themselves. The verb is of the form iftaʿala (yaftaʿilūna) from the root "du'ā'" (calling, asking), like ishtawā and ijtamala, meaning "he roasted" and "he beautified for himself." Or it means what they mutually call for, as in your saying "irtamūhu," meaning "tarāmawhu" (they threw it to one another). Or it means what they wish for (yatamannawna), from their saying "ud'u ʿalayya mā shi'ta" (ask of me whatever you wish), meaning "tamannahu ʿalayya" (wish it upon me). Or it means what they asked for in the world of the Garden and its ranks. "Mā" is either a relative pronoun (mawṣūla) or a descriptive (mawṣūfa), in the nominative case as the subject (mubtadaʾ), and "lahum" (for them) is its predicate (khabar).

﴿Peace﴾ (salām): it is either a substitute (badal) for it or another descriptive (ṣifa). It is permissible that it be its predicate, or that its predicate be omitted, or that it be a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is omitted, meaning "and for them is peace." It is also read in the accusative (naṣb), as an infinitive of emphasis (maṣdar) or a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning "for them is what they desire, purely."

﴿A word from a Lord, Most Merciful.﴾ That is, Allah says, or it is said to them, a word proceeding from Him. The meaning is that Allah greets them, through the angels or without intermediary, honouring them, and that is what they seek and desire. Its accusative (naṣb) is also possible, as a particularizing accusative (ikhtiṣāṣ).

﴿And separate yourselves today, O guilty ones﴾: withdraw from the believers. This will be when they are driven to Paradise, like His saying: ﴿And on the day the Hour is established, on that day they will be divided﴾. It was said: "Withdraw from all good," or "Separate yourselves in the Fire, for every disbeliever has a house in which he is alone; he neither sees nor is seen."

﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan﴾: this is among what will be said to them as rebuke and as the establishing of proof against them (ilzām al-ḥujjah). His "charge" to them is the rational and revealed proofs set up for them, which command His worship, forbid the worship of others, and make that worship the worship of Satan, because he is the one who commands it and makes it attractive. It has been read as "iʿhad" with the vowel of the imperfect prefix changed, and as "aḥhad" and "aḥad," in the dialect of the Banu Tamim.

﴿Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you﴾: this is a reason for the prohibition against worshipping him, through obedience to him in what he drives them to.

﴿And that you should worship Me﴾: this is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "that you should not worship." ﴿This is a straight path﴾: the demonstrative refers either to what was charged to them or to the worship of Him. So the sentence is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf) explaining what required the charge in both its parts, or in its other part. The indefiniteness (tankīr) is for emphasis and magnification, or for partialness, since monotheism is the traversing of only part of the straight path. (p-272)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 62–64:

﴿And he had certainly led astray from among you a great multitude. Did you not then use reason?﴾ This is a return to explaining the enmity of Satan, along with the clarity of his enmity and the obviousness of his misguidance to anyone who has even the least intellect and judgment. Al-jibill (الجِبِلّ) means the creation. Ya'qub read it with two dammas, and Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with both dammas with the lam lightened (takhfif). Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read it with one damma and a sukun, with lightening. All of these are dialects (lughat). It has also been read as "jibillan" (جِبِلًّا), the plural of jibillah, like khilqah and khalq, and as "jilan" (جِيلًا), the singular of al-ajyal (generations).

﴿This is Hell, which you were promised.﴾

﴿Burn in it today for what you used to deny.﴾ Taste its heat today because of your disbelief in the world.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 65–66:

﴿Today We shall seal their mouths﴾ We will prevent them from speaking. ﴿and their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn﴾ through the appearance of the traces of sins upon them and their indication of the deeds, or by God making them speak. And in a hadith: "They will deny and dispute, so their mouths will be sealed, and their hands and feet will speak."

﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾ We would have wiped out their eyes until they become effaced. ﴿So they would race to the path﴾ so they would race toward the way they were accustomed to traveling. Its being in the accusative (intisab) is either by removing the preposition, or by implying in "racing" the meaning of "hastening" (ibtidar), or by treating the object reached as the one raced to in an extended sense, or by the adverbial construction (zarf). ﴿Then how would they see?﴾ The path and the direction of travel, let alone anything else.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 67–68:

﴿And if We willed, We would surely transform them﴾ by altering their forms and nullifying their powers. ﴿In their places﴾, meaning in their place, such that they would be petrified therein. Abu Bakr recited "makanatihim" (in their places, plural).

﴿So they would not be able to proceed﴾, that is, to go forth. ﴿Nor would they return﴾, nor return. The verb is placed here for the sake of the rhyme (fawasil). It was also said that ﴿nor would they return﴾ means they would not return from their disbelief. It is also recited "mudiyyan" (with the mim taken with the dad kasra, the waw being changed to ya, as in "al-ʿitiyy" and "al-ʿutiyy"), and "madiyyan" (like "sabiyy"). The meaning is that, through their disbelief and their breaking of what was covenanted to them, they deserve to be dealt with in that way; but We have not done so, because of the all-encompassing mercy toward them and because wisdom requires that they be granted respite.

﴿And whomever We grant long life﴾, meaning whomever We prolong the life of, ﴿We reverse him in creation﴾, meaning We turn him over in it, so that his weakness and the disintegration of his body and powers keep increasing, the reverse of what he was at the beginning of his affair. Ibn Kathir, following this reading, pronounces the damma of the ha' fully in accordance with its original form. Asim and Hamza recited "nunakkishu" (from tankis), which is more emphatic, while al-nakss is more common.

﴿Will they not then understand?﴾ That the One who is able to do this is able to effect the obliteration and transformation, since it includes both and more, except that it is done gradually. Nafi', through the transmission of Ibn Amir, Ibn Dhakwan and Yaqub recited it with the ta' (ta'qilun), because the address preceding it is in the second person.

﴿And whomever We grant long life﴾, meaning whomever We prolong the life of, ﴿We reverse him in creation﴾, meaning We turn him over in it, so that his weakness and the disintegration of his body and powers keep increasing, the reverse of what he was at the beginning of his affair. Ibn Kathir, following this reading, pronounces the damma of the ha' fully in accordance with its original form. Asim and Hamza recited "nunakkishu" (from tankis), which is more emphatic, while al-nakss is more common.

﴿Will they not then understand?﴾ That the One who is able to do this is able to effect the obliteration and transformation, since it includes both and more, except that it is done gradually. Nafi', through the transmission of Ibn Amir, Ibn Dhakwan and Yaqub recited it with the ta' (ta'qilun), because the address preceding it is in the second person.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 69–70:

﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾: a refutation of their claim that Muhammad is a poet; that is, We did not teach him poetry through the teaching of the Qur'an, for it does not resemble poetry in wording or meaning, since it is neither rhymed (muqaffa) nor metrical (mawzun). Nor is its meaning what poets aim at in imaginative depictions that encourage or deter, and the like.

﴿And it is not befitting for him﴾: that is, poetry is not proper for him and would not come easily to him if he intended to compose it, given what you know of his disposition over some forty years. As for his peace and blessings be upon him saying: «I am the Prophet, there is no lie; I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muttalib», and his saying:

"Are you anything but a finger that has bled,
and in the way of God you have suffered what you have suffered"

these are accidental, without artifice or intention on his part to that end, and the like of this often occurs within prose. Moreover, al-Khalil did not count the half-line (mashtur) of rajaz as poetry. It has also been related that he vocalized the two bāʾs with a fatḥa and vocalized the first tāʾ with a kasra without lengthening it, and made the second sakin. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to "Qur'an," that is, it is not befitting for the Qur'an to be poetry. ﴿It is nothing but a reminder﴾: an admonition and guidance from God, exalted is He.

﴿And a clear Qur'an﴾: a heavenly book recited in places of worship; it is evident that it is not the speech of humans, because of the inimitability (iʿjaz) that it contains.

﴿That he may warn﴾: the Qur'an or the Messenger ﷺ; this is supported by the reading of Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and Yaʿqub with the letter tāʾ. ﴿him who is alive﴾: one who is intelligent and perceptive, for the heedless is like the dead; or one who is a believer in the knowledge of God, exalted is He, for eternal life is through faith. The restriction of the warning to him is because he is the one who benefits from it. ﴿And the word may be fulfilled﴾: and the word of punishment becomes due. ﴿against the disbelievers﴾: those persisting in disbelief. He placed them in opposition to "him who is alive," indicating that because of their disbelief, the fall of their argument, and their failure to reflect, they are in reality dead.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 71–73:

﴿Do they not see that We have created for them, of what Our hands have wrought, cattle, so that they are their owners?﴾ "Of what Our hands have wrought" means: of that which We alone undertook to originate, and which none other than Us has the power to originate. The mention of "hands" and the attribution of the act to them is a metaphor (isti'arah) that conveys an intensified emphasis on exclusivity and sole origination. ﴿Cattle﴾: He singled them out for mention because of the marvels of their natural design and the abundance of their benefits. ﴿So they are their owners﴾: they possess them by Our having granted them ownership, or they are able to control them and dispose of them by Our subjecting them to them. He said:

I no longer bear arms, nor do I... own the camel's halter if it bolts.

﴿And We have made them subservient to them﴾: We have made them submissive to them. ﴿Of them is their ride﴾: their means of riding. It is read as "rakūbatuhum," which has the same meaning as "ḥalūb" and "ḥalūbah" (milch animal). It is also said that rukūb is its plural, or that it means "one who is ridden," or: "from their benefits is their riding." ﴿And of them they eat﴾: that is, they eat their flesh.

﴿And for them in them are benefits﴾: from their hides, wool and fleece. ﴿And drinks﴾: from their milk; mashārib is the plural of mashrab meaning "place," or it is a verbal noun. Ibn 'Amir alone, through the transmission of Hisham, inclined the shin (sheen) in it. ﴿Will they not then give thanks?﴾ for the blessings of God in this, for were it not for His creating them and subjecting them to them, it would not have been possible to obtain these important benefits.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 74–76:

﴿And they took besides Allah gods, that they might be helped.﴾ They associated them with Him in worship after they had seen from Him that overwhelming power and those manifest blessings, and they knew that He alone is the One who possesses them. ﴿That perhaps they might be helped.﴾ (They hoped) that they would help them in the matters that afflicted them, whereas the reality is the reverse, because (p-274)

﴿They are not able to help them, and they are for them⦅their gods⦆ a host brought forward.﴾ ﴿A host brought forward﴾ means prepared to guard them and defend them; or (the reading is) "muhdirun" (bringing forward), i.e., they will be brought forward (as) those who are made to attend them in the Fire.

﴿So let not their speech grieve you.﴾ ﴿Let not grieve you﴾ means let it not concern you. It is also read with a damma on the yaʾ, from aḥzana (to cause grief). ﴿Their speech﴾ refers to their blasphemy against Allah through atheism and associationism, or against you through denial and disparagement. ﴿Indeed, We know what they conceal and what they reveal.﴾ So We will recompense them for it, and this suffices for you to find consolation in it. This is an explanation of the prohibition, given as a new statement (istiʾnaf); for this reason, if it were read ﴿inna﴾ with a fatḥa, by omitting the lam of causation, it would also be permissible.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 77–78:

﴿Has not man considered that We created him from a drop [of semen], and then he is an open adversary?﴾ This is a second consolation, by belittling what they say in relation to their denial of the Resurrection. It also contains a severe reproach of his denial, in that He marvelled at it and made it an evident excess in contention, and a contradiction to the denial of the power to do what is easier than what He did at the beginning of his creation, and a repayment of the blessing which has no greater [blessing] beyond it, namely that He created him from the most base and humble of things, [yet] he, honored and noble, responds with disobedience and denial.

It is narrated that Ubayy ibn Khalaf came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a decayed bone, crumbling it with his hand, and said: "Do you think that Allah will revive this after it has decayed?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Yes. He will resurrect you and cause you to enter the Fire." So this was revealed.

It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿then he is an open adversary﴾ is: then he, after having been a despised fluid, becomes one who discerns, speaks, is capable of disputation, and expresses what is in his soul.

﴿And he sets forth for Us a comparison﴾: a strange matter, namely the negation of the power to revive the dead, or his likening Him to His creation by describing Him with incapacity in that which they were incapable of. ﴿And forgets his creation﴾: Our creating him. ﴿He says, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?"﴾ denying it and deeming it far-fetched. The *rameem* (decayed) is what has rotted of the bones; perhaps it is *fa'eel* in the sense of *fa'il*, having become a noun by predominance, and for this reason it is not feminine; or it is in the sense of *maf'ool* from *ramamtuhu*. In this is evidence that the bone has life, so death affects it as it affects the other limbs.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 79–80:

﴿Say: He will give them life who brought them into being the first time.﴾ For His power is as it was, since change is impossible in it, and the matter remains in its state of receptivity, which is necessary to its essence. ﴿And He is Knowledgeable of every creation.﴾ He knows the details of created things by His knowledge and how they were created. So He knows the scattered, dispersed parts of persons, their roots, their distinctions, their places, and the way to distinguish them. He joins some of them to others according to the previous pattern, and restores the accidents and powers that were in them, or produces their like.

﴿He who made for you fire from the green tree﴾, such as the marakh (a tree whose wood is used for kindling) and the 'ifar (another such tree). ﴿Fire﴾: by rubbing the marakh against the 'ifar, while both are green and water drips from them, so that the fire is struck. ﴿Then from it you kindle.﴾ You have no doubt that it is fire that comes out of it. So whoever is able to produce fire from the green tree, despite the watery nature in it that is opposed to fire in its quality, is more able to restore freshness to what was fresh, then dried out and decayed.

It was also read as «مِنَ الشَّجَرِ الخَضْراءِ» (min al-shajari al-khadra'i, with the feminine form), according to the sense, like His saying ﴿So they will fill their bellies from it﴾ (فَمالِئُونَ مِنها البُطُونَ).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verses 81–82:

﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth⦅—despite the immensity of their bodies and the greatness of their station—⦆ ﴿able to create the likes of them?﴾ ⦅The likes of them⦆ in smallness and insignificance relative to them; or ⦅the likes of them⦆ in the essential fundamentals of their substance and their attributes, and that is the resurrection (al-ma'ad). It is related from Ya'qub (Ya‘qūb) that he read «yaqdiru» (يَقْدِرُ).

﴿Yes⦆ is an answer from God Most High affirming what follows a negation, indicating that there is no answer other than it. ﴿And He is the All-Creating, the All-Knowing﴾, abundant in created things (al-makhluqat) and known things (al-ma'lumat).

﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it: "Be!"﴾ meaning: His affair is only this. ﴿And it is⦆ — that is, it comes into being, i.e., it occurs. This is an illustration of the effect of His power on what He wills by means of the command of one obeyed to one who obeys, in the attainment of what is commanded, without refusal, hesitation, or need to undertake an action or employ an instrument, cutting off the basis of doubt. It is an analogy of God Most High's power to the power of creatures. Ibn 'Amir (Ibn ‘Āmir) and al-Kisa'i (al-Kisā'ī) read it in the accusative (fa-yakūna·n), as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon (yaqūla).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 83:

﴿So glory be to Him in whose hand is the dominion (malakut) of all things﴾. It is a declaration of His transcendence above what they ascribe to Him, and an expression of wonder at what they say about Him, justified by His being the Owner of the whole affair and Capable of everything. ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾: a promise and a warning for those who affirm and those who deny. Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the ta' (turja'una, "you are returned").

And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "I did not know what was narrated about the virtue of Ya-Sin, how it was singled out for it, until I found that it is this verse."

And from him, upon him be blessings and peace, [he said]: "Indeed every thing has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin. Whoever Muslim recites it seeking thereby the Face of Allah, Allah will forgive him, and he will be given a reward as if he had recited the Qur'an twenty-two times. And whichever Muslim has Surah Ya-Sin recited in his presence when the Angel of Death descends upon him, ten angels descend for each letter of it, standing before him in rows, sending blessings upon him and asking forgiveness for him, and they witness his washing, follow his funeral procession, pray over him, and witness his burial. And whichever Muslim recites Ya-Sin while in the agonies of death, the Angel of Death will not take his soul until Ridwan comes to him with a drink from Paradise, and he drinks it while on his bed, and then his soul is taken while he is sated, and he remains in his grave sated, and he will not need any of the pools of the Prophets until he enters Paradise sated."
